## Why there has to be a matrix

Time has an order and a direction: 1999 comes before 2000, and the past
can move the future but not the reverse. A cross-section of states has
neither. Arizona is not "before" Nevada, and if Nevada's prices move
Arizona's, Arizona's move Nevada's in the same year. To say anything
about dependence across units, the analyst has to supply the order that
time supplies for free: a statement of which units are close to which,
and how close. That statement is the **spatial weights matrix** W, N × N,
with $w_{ij}$ the weight of unit *j* in unit *i*'s row and zeros on the
diagonal.

Nothing in the data produces W. It is chosen, and @anselin1988 [p. 19]
calls that choice "one of the most controversial subjects in spatial
econometrics". Every estimate in this chapter is an estimate *given W*.

## 1. Three ways to say neighbour

**Contiguity.** $w_{ij} = 1$ when *i* and *j* share a border, 0
otherwise; "queen" contiguity counts a shared corner as a border, "rook"
does not. This is `usaw49` for the states and `riceww` for the farms,
where the border is "same village". Binary contiguity imposes the least
structure, makes $Wy$ the plain average of the neighbours, and is the
usual choice when the aim is to *test* for spatial effects rather than to
estimate a theoretically given process [@anselin1988, p. 21; @croissant2019,
sec. 10.2].

**Nearest neighbours.** $w_{ij} = 1$ for the *k* units closest to *i*.
Every unit gets exactly *k* neighbours, which keeps W balanced where units
differ wildly in size, at the price of links that cross no border, as the
long lines in the West of the [weights section](index.qmd#sec-sp-weights)
show.

**Distance.** $w_{ij} = 1$, or $1/d_{ij}$, for every *j* within a cutoff
of *i*, so that influence fades with distance and the cutoff says where it
stops. Dense where units are small, thin where they are large.

Whichever is chosen, the chapter assumes that W is **exogenous** and
**fixed over time**. Geography is exogenous; a matrix of bilateral trade
shares, built from the same economy as the outcome, is not
[@croissant2019, sec. 10.2]. The distance need not be geographic: a space
of economic or demographic characteristics works the same way, as long
as it is not an outcome of the model.

## 2. Row standardisation and what ρ means

Dividing each row by its sum makes $\sum_j w_{ij} = 1$, and then

$$
(Wy)_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\, y_j
$$

is the average outcome of *i*'s neighbours. The spatial parameter ρ then
reads as a share: ρ = 0.65 on the defactored house-price residuals means a
state's residual carries 0.65 of its neighbours' average residual. Two
costs. W stops being symmetric: Maine has one neighbour and gives it
weight 1; New Hampshire has three and gives Maine 1/3. And ρ stops being
comparable across matrices: with four nearest neighbours every weight is
0.25, with a distance band the average weight is whatever the density
makes it, and the same data return a different ρ̂ under each. The chapter
reports every ρ̂ as a number for `usaw49`.

## 3. The parameter space

A spatial lag or error model has to invert $I - \rho W$. The inverse
exists whenever ρ is not the reciprocal of an eigenvalue of W, so the
admissible interval around zero runs from $1/\omega_{\min}$ to
$1/\omega_{\max}$, with ω the real eigenvalues. For a row-standardised W,
$\omega_{\max} = 1$, so the upper bound is 1; the lower bound is whatever
the most negative eigenvalue gives, −1.39 for `usaw49`.

A bound that needs no eigenvalues is [@kelejian2010; @pesaran2015,
p. 799]

$$
|\rho| < \frac{1}{\tau^*}, \qquad
\tau^* = \min\big(\lVert W\rVert_1, \lVert W\rVert_\infty\big),
$$

the smaller of the largest column sum and the largest row sum. With rows
standardised, $\lVert W\rVert_\infty = 1$ and so $\tau^* \le 1$: any
$|\rho| < 1$ is safe. The familiar statement "ρ lies in (−1, 1)" is exact
only when W is row *and* column standardised [@pesaran2015, p. 802], and
`usaw49`'s column sums run from 0.33 to 1.7.

The eigenvalues matter for a second reason. The likelihood of every model
in this chapter carries $\ln|I - \rho W| = \sum_i \ln(1 - \rho\,\omega_i)$,
and `spml`'s default `method = "eigen"` computes exactly that sum at every
step of the optimiser. For N in the thousands the eigenvalues are too
expensive, and the sparse-matrix and Chebyshev approximations take over
[@millo2012, sec. 5.2].

## 4. Granularity: why a lag is endogenous

A spatial lag $Wy$ is endogenous, and a within fit that includes it is
biased, because $y_j$ for a neighbour *j* contains $u_j$, which is
correlated with $u_i$ through the same W. @pesaran2015 [p. 800] make the
condition precise: the covariance of $(Wy)_{it}$ with $u_{it}$ stays away
from zero only when the weights are **non-granular**, that is, when some
$w_{ij}$ stay bounded away from zero as N grows. If every weight were of
order $1/N$, the lag would be a cross-section average, its covariance
with any one unit's error would vanish, and there would be nothing to
instrument.

This is the bridge to the [previous
chapter](../02-cross-dependence/theory-cross-sectional-dependence.qmd). A
cross-section average *is* a spatial lag with a granular W, every weight
$1/N$; it proxies a factor that every unit loads on, and CCE puts it on
the right-hand side as an exogenous control. A contiguity W, with a
handful of weights near 1/4 in every row, is the opposite case: its lag
is endogenous, the dependence it generates is weak, and α stays below 1
[@pesaran2015, sec. 30.3.3]. The largest weight in `usaw49` is 1, Maine's.

## 5. Sparsity: what the model links

W is sparse: 9% of `usaw49` is non-zero. The covariance of a spatial
error model is not. With $u = (I - \lambda W)^{-1}\varepsilon$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(u) = \sigma^2 \big[(I - \lambda W)'(I - \lambda W)\big]^{-1},
$$

and the inverse of a sparse matrix is dense: 99.7% of the cells of
$(I - 0.5W)^{-1}$ are non-zero. A shock in California reaches Maine, in
any spatial autoregressive model, through the chain of neighbours in
between [@pesaran2015, p. 801]. Two alternative error forms keep the
covariance as sparse as W: the spatial moving average, $u = \varepsilon +
\lambda W\varepsilon$, and the spatial error components model, $u = W\xi +
\varepsilon$ [@pesaran2015, eqs. 30.5–30.6]. They say a shock stops at the
first neighbour. Neither is implemented in **splm**, whose
`spatial.error` is the autoregressive form only, so the sharpest
distinction in the theory is not available to the code.

## If / then

| If | Then |
|---|---|
| The question is whether space matters at all | Binary contiguity, row-standardised [@anselin1988, p. 21] |
| Units differ wildly in size | *k* nearest neighbours; say what *k* and why |
| A ρ̂ is reported above 1 | The fit is broken, or W is not row-standardised; check $\lVert W\rVert_\infty$ |
| Two papers report ρ̂ on different W | They are not comparable; compare the impacts instead ([effects](index.qmd#sec-sp-impacts)) |
| W is built from an outcome of the model (trade, migration) | It is endogenous; the chapter's estimators do not apply |
| Every weight is of order 1/N | The lag is a cross-section average, and the question is a factor, not space |
| A shock should stop at the first neighbour | The autoregressive error is the wrong form, and the right one is not implemented: say so |
